Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers

Amitakshar Biswas ††thanks: Corresponding author: biswas8@illinois.edu    Ruoqing Zhu Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
Abstract

We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an ’approximate conditional-gradient step’ for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.

Keywords: Off-policy evaluation, contextual bandits, multiple loggers, data acquisition, experimental design, adaptive inference

1 Introduction

Contextual bandits are widely used in applications where an action must be chosen after observing information about the current user or environment, including recommendation systems, online content selection, and personalized interventions (Li et al., 2010; Tewari and Murphy, 2017). In such applications a new policy usually cannot be deployed simply to learn how well it performs, since online experimentation is costly, risky, and slow. Off-policy evaluation avoids this by estimating the value of a target policy from data collected under a different behavior policy (Dudík et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).

In practice, the available data need not come from a single behavior policy. Deployed systems are updated over time, several experiments may run in parallel, and different loggers may use different decision rules. Methods for combining observations from several loggers generally take the logger sample sizes as given (Agarwal et al., 2017; He et al., 2019; Kallus et al., 2021). In many applications, however, more data can still be collected, but only from loggers that already exist, and these loggers differ both in the actions they tend to take and in their per-observation prices. An inexpensive logger may concentrate on a few actions, while a more costly logger may provide the coverage that a target policy needs. The practical question is where the remaining observations should be purchased when the reward distribution is not yet known. We study a fixed set of logging policies μ1,…,μK\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{K} with known costs c1,…,cKc_{1},\ldots,c_{K}. The policies cannot be redesigned, and acquisition chooses only which logger to sample from next, subject to a finite budget.

This problem differs from behavior-policy design, in which the logging or augmentation policy is itself chosen to reduce the variance of a downstream estimator (Hanna et al., 2024; Tucker and Joachims, 2023; Mukherjee et al., 2024b). When the loggers are fixed, an allocation is a count vector N=(N1,…,NK)∈ℤ+KN=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{K})\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{K} with c⊤​N≤Bc^{\top}N\leq B, where NkN_{k} is the number of observations purchased from logger kk and BB is the total budget. Each purchase increments one coordinate of NN and bears the corresponding logger cost.

A second feature is that several target policies may have to be evaluated from the same sample. We consider a finite target class Π={π1,…,πM}\Pi=\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{M}\} and seek a design that controls the largest target-specific uncertainty over that class. The criterion retains each policy’s target-specific efficient variance and minimizes its maximum, so the objective can change as the target attaining that maximum changes. Prior work on evaluating multiple policies jointly provides related motivation, although it studies different sampling settings and objectives (Dann et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025).

The criterion depends on the conditional reward mean and variance, which are unknown at the outset and must be estimated from the observations acquired along the way. We propose a sequential rule, which we call Adaptive Greedy, that re-estimates the criterion as data accrue and at each step purchases from the affordable logger with the largest estimated reduction in the worst-target criterion per unit of cost. An additional feature is that the rule does not plan toward a declared final budget. The budget enters only through which loggers remain affordable and when acquisition stops. This is useful if the available budget is unexpectedly reduced or the process must stop early, since the data already collected were chosen to improve the current design rather than to follow a plan optimized for a larger final budget. Planners that repeatedly solve for count vectors at a declared final budget behave differently, since their early purchases are chosen with that budget in mind.

For a fixed logger composition, weighting each observation by the overall mixture of the logging policies has no larger asymptotic variance than weighting it only by the logger that generated it. We therefore combine all acquired observations using this pooled estimator. Under adaptive data collection, however, the final logger composition depends on the rewards observed along the way, so the pooled denominator is itself random. We show that as the design converges, this random denominator can be replaced at first order by its deterministic limiting value. As a result, the pooled estimator remains asymptotically normal and its large-sample variance is determined by the allocation reached by the algorithm.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate budgeted off-policy evaluation as a sequential allocation problem among loggers with heterogeneous costs and propose the Adaptive Greedy algorithm. Second, assuming overlap only for the pooled behavior distribution at the optimal design, rather than for every logger, we show that the resulting design converges almost surely to the continuous minimax design. Under stronger conditions on the plug-in estimates, we also derive an explicit polynomial rate. Third, we establish joint asymptotic normality and consistent covariance estimation for the pooled estimator, even though the logger choices depend on previously observed rewards. The variance advantage of pooled over logger-specific weighting is known for fixed designs (Agarwal et al., 2017; Kallus et al., 2021). Our result shows that pooled inference remains valid after adaptive data collection under the stated conditions.

1.1 Related Work

Off-policy evaluation from several loggers has so far been studied with the logger sample sizes given in advance. Agarwal et al. (2017) observe that weighting each observation by the pooled behavior distribution never increases variance relative to weighting it by the logger that generated it. He et al. (2019) study off-policy learning from data collected by multiple loggers, and Lai et al. (2020) choose variance-minimizing weights for combining estimators computed from several behavior policies. Kallus et al. (2021) characterize the semiparametric efficiency bound for the fixed-stratified multi-logger model and construct an estimator that attains it. This pooled bound, viewed as a function of the logger composition, is the population objective of our design problem. Related mixture-design problems have also been studied in importance sampling. He and Owen (2014) establish convexity of variance objectives for mixtures of fixed proposal distributions and discuss minimizing the maximum variance when estimating multiple integrals from shared samples. Our setting instead concerns sequential purchases from fixed contextual-bandit loggers with heterogeneous costs, where allocation decisions depend on the observations acquired so far.

A second line of work designs or learns the data-collection policy itself for downstream evaluation. Examples include behavior-policy search (Hanna et al., 2024; Liu and Zhang, 2024), experimental design in linear heteroscedastic bandits (Mukherjee et al., 2024b), safe or robust data-collection designs (Zhu and Kveton, 2022; Mukherjee et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026), and the optimization of logging probabilities (Douglas et al., 2026). In contextual bandits, Tucker and Joachims (2023) design an augmentation logging policy for an existing dataset and evaluate with a balanced estimator that divides by the pooled behavior distribution of the original and augmentation data. In all of these works the behavior or augmentation policy is a design variable, whereas in our setting the loggers are fixed and only the number of purchases from each can be chosen.

Evaluating several target policies from shared data is a closely related problem. Dann et al. (2023) study high-confidence evaluation of multiple policies in episodic reinforcement learning, Jain et al. (2024) adaptively learn a behavior policy for evaluating several general value functions, and Chen et al. (2025) optimize an offline sampling distribution for several policies in an episodic MDP. Liu et al. (2025a) and Russo and Pacchiano (2025) also study data collection when there are several evaluation targets. These works motivate designing for a finite target class jointly, which in our setting takes the form of a minimax criterion over the target-specific pooled efficiency bounds.

Inference from data collected by outcome-adaptive rules has been developed for batched bandits, adaptive experiments, and off-policy evaluation from contextual bandits (Zhang et al., 2020; Hadad et al., 2021; Zhan et al., 2021; Bibaut et al., 2021; Waudby-Smith et al., 2024). In these works the weights and normalizations entering the estimator are predictable, meaning that they are known when each observation is collected, and martingale arguments apply to the resulting estimating equations. The pooled estimator studied here divides by the final logger composition, which depends on rewards observed along the acquisition path and is known only after acquisition ends. Design convergence allows us to replace this random final mixture by its deterministic limit.

The cost-normalized feasible set and the minimax variance criterion connect the problem to classical optimal design (Fedorov, 1972; Pukelsheim, 2006). The sequential update has a conditional-gradient interpretation related to the Fedorov–Wynn design algorithms (Wynn, 1970; Chernoff, 1959), with vertices fixed by the available loggers and a step size set by the cost of the logger purchased. Section 4.1 develops this connection.

2 Preliminaries

The context distribution PXP_{X} and conditional reward distribution PRP_{R} are common across loggers. Data are acquired sequentially, and each logger is chosen using only the data observed before that choice. For observation ii, let Ki∈{1,…,K}K_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,K\} denote the selected logger, and AiA_{i} for the contextual-bandit action generated by that logger. Let

2.2 Fixed Logger Sizes

The purpose of this subsection is to obtain the variance criterion that we will later use for acquisition. Here we fix the sample size tt and the sequence of loggers k1,…,ktk_{1},\ldots,k_{t} with ki∈{1,…,K}k_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,K\}. Let Nk=Nt,kN_{k}=N_{t,k} be the resulting number of observations from logger kk, and N=(N1,…,NK)⊤N=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{K})^{\top}. Thus ∑kNk=t\sum_{k}N_{k}=t, the counts are deterministic, and no acquisition decision depends on the observed data. This is the fixed-stratified setting studied by Kallus et al. (2021).

Since all loggers share PXP_{X} and PRP_{R}, we can weight every observation by the mixture of the logging policies, as if the combined sample came from that mixture. This weighting never gives a larger variance than weighting each observation by the logger that generated it (Agarwal et al., 2017; Kallus et al., 2021). The mixture is the pooled behavior distribution

μ¯N​(a∣x)=1t​∑k=1KNk​μk​(a∣x).\bar{\mu}_{N}(a\mid x)=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x). (2.2)

We define the pooled augmented inverse propensity weighted (AIPW) estimator of JjJ_{j} as

J~t,j=1t​∑i=1t[qj​(Xi)+πj​(Ai∣Xi)μ¯N​(Ai∣Xi)​{Ri−q⁡(Xi,Ai)}].\widetilde{J}_{t,j}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[q_{j}(X_{i})+\frac{\pi_{j}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{\bar{\mu}_{N}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}\{R_{i}-q(X_{i},A_{i})\}\right]. (2.3)

Kallus et al. (2021, Theorem 1) show that this weighting, together with the true qq, minimizes variance within the estimator class in the fixed-stratified setting.

For a fixed logger sequence k1,…,ktk_{1},\ldots,k_{t} with ess​inf𝒮⁡μ¯N>0\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{\mathcal{S}}\bar{\mu}_{N}>0, the pooled estimator is unbiased, 𝔼⁡(J~t,j)=Jj\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{J}_{t,j})=J_{j}, and its fixed-design variance is

Var⁡(J~t,j)=Var⁡{qj​(X)}t+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜πj​(a∣X)2​σ2​(X,a)∑k=1KNk​μk​(a∣X).\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde{J}_{t,j})=\frac{\operatorname{Var}\{q_{j}(X)\}}{t}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\pi_{j}(a\mid X)^{2}\sigma^{2}(X,a)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid X)}. (2.4)

This variance formula follows from Kallus et al. (2021, Theorem 1). For notational convenience, let Vj=Var⁡{qj​(X)}V_{j}=\mathrm{Var}\{q_{j}(X)\} and Wj​(x,a)=πj​(a∣x)2​σ2​(x,a)W_{j}(x,a)=\pi_{j}(a\mid x)^{2}\sigma^{2}(x,a). Note that the variance does not depend on the order in which the loggers appear but only through the count vector NN. Write θk=Nk/t\theta_{k}=N_{k}/t for the sample fractions, which lie in the simplex 𝒮K={θ∈ℝ+K:𝟏⊤​θ=1}\mathcal{S}_{K}=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}:\mathbf{1}^{\top}\theta=1\}, so that μ¯N=mθ\bar{\mu}_{N}=m_{\theta} with mθ​(a∣x)=∑k=1Kθk​μk​(a∣x)m_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x). Then (2.4) becomes Var⁡(J~t,j)=Aj​(θ)/t\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{J}_{t,j})=A_{j}(\theta)/t with

Aj​(θ)=Vj+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)mθ​(a∣X).A_{j}(\theta)=V_{j}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{W_{j}(X,a)}{m_{\theta}(a\mid X)}. (2.5)

Thus, for a fixed logger composition θ\theta, a smaller Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta) means a smaller variance for estimating JjJ_{j}.

Kallus et al. (2021, Theorem 4) derive the efficient influence function and the semiparametric efficiency bound for the fixed-stratified multi-logger model. Their bound for πj\pi_{j} is exactly Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta). Hence Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta) is the smallest regular asymptotic variance attainable for estimating JjJ_{j} under a fixed logger composition θ\theta with ess​inf𝒮⁡mθ>0\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{\mathcal{S}}m_{\theta}>0.11 1 Kallus et al. (2021, Theorem 5) further show that the efficiency bound is unchanged when the logging policies are unknown. This efficiency result is for the fixed-stratified setting and does not automatically extend to our adaptive procedure, where the final logger composition depends on the observed data. We nevertheless use Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta) to construct the acquisition objective, and we establish valid post-acquisition inference in Section 4.2 for the pooled estimator computed from the acquired sample.

3 Methodology

In this section, we develop our sequential method, Adaptive Greedy. We break it into three parts: Section 3.1 defines the design criterion that we eventually minimize, Section 3.2 describes our greedy approach to selecting the loggers adaptively and how we estimate the unknown quantities, and finally, we state the complete algorithm in Section 3.3. All proofs and derivations are provided in the appendices.

3.1 Design Criterion

To compare allocations and decide where the next observation is most useful, we use the variance formula (2.4) as our criterion, with constants added so that it is finite at N=0N=0. Let N=(N1,…,NK)⊤N=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{K})^{\top} be a count vector. For target policy πj\pi_{j}, we define

Gj​(N)=Vj𝟏⊤​N+η0+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)DN​(X,a),G_{j}(N)=\frac{V_{j}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}N+\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{W_{j}(X,a)}{D_{N}(X,a)}, (3.1)

where DN​(x,a)=η+∑k=1KNk​μk​(a∣x)D_{N}(x,a)=\eta+\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x) and η,η0>0\eta,\eta_{0}>0. In our experiments we use the simple choice η=η0=1\eta=\eta_{0}=1 throughout. Since every target in Π\Pi should be estimated accurately, we control the worst target-specific variance G⁡(N)=max1≤j≤M⁡Gj​(N)G(N)=\max_{1\leq j\leq M}G_{j}(N). Other choices can also be considered, for example M−1​∑j=1MGj​(N)M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{M}G_{j}(N), but the average can be small while one target is estimated poorly. Note that a new observation reduces the variance if it adds coverage for regions where DN​(x,a)D_{N}(x,a) is small and Wj​(X,a)W_{j}(X,a) is large.

To compare allocations independently of how much has been spent, we normalize the counts by their cost. Define zN=N/CNz_{N}=N/C_{N}, where CN=c⊤​NC_{N}=c^{\top}N is the total expenditure. Thus zN,kz_{N,k} is the number of observations purchased from logger kk per unit of spent budget. Since c⊤​zN=1c^{\top}z_{N}=1, let 𝒞={z∈ℝ+K:c⊤​z=1}\mathcal{C}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}:c^{\top}z=1\}. Multiplying Gj​(N)G_{j}(N) by the spent budget CNC_{N} removes the decrease in variance that comes simply from spending more money. For a large spent budget, CN​Gj​(N)≈𝒢j​(zN)C_{N}G_{j}(N)\approx\mathcal{G}_{j}(z_{N}), where 𝒢j,𝒢:𝒞→ℝ∪{∞}\mathcal{G}_{j},\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} are

𝒢j​(z)=Vj𝟏⊤​z+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)𝝁​(X,a)⊤​z,𝒢⁡(z)=max1≤j≤M⁡𝒢j​(z),z∈𝒞,\mathcal{G}_{j}(z)=\frac{V_{j}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}z}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{W_{j}(X,a)}{\bm{\mu}(X,a)^{\top}z},\qquad\mathcal{G}(z)=\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\mathcal{G}_{j}(z),\qquad z\in\mathcal{C}, (3.2)

with 𝝁⁡(x,a)=(μ1​(a∣x),…,μK​(a∣x))⊤\bm{\mu}(x,a)=(\mu_{1}(a\mid x),\ldots,\mu_{K}(a\mid x))^{\top}. For any fixed positive lower bound on the pooled coverage, Lemma A3.8 shows that there is a finite constant KGK_{G} such that

|CN​Gj​(N)−𝒢j​(zN)|≤KGCN\left|C_{N}G_{j}(N)-\mathcal{G}_{j}(z_{N})\right|\leq\frac{K_{G}}{C_{N}}

for every nonzero count vector with such coverage. We will work with Gj​(N)G_{j}(N) for our algorithm as it is more convenient and we will use 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} when we talk about convergence in Section 4.

We now define the optimal allocation we would like our algorithm to converge to. Since each 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} is convex in 𝒞\mathcal{C} whenever the denominator is positive (as Vj≥0V_{j}\geq 0, Wj​(X,a)≥0W_{j}(X,a)\geq 0, and x↦1/xx\mapsto 1/x is convex for x>0x>0), 𝒢=maxj⁡𝒢j\mathcal{G}=\max_{j}\mathcal{G}_{j} is also convex. If VjV_{j} and WjW_{j} are known, define

z⋆∈arg⁡minv∈𝒞⁡𝒢⁡(v),θ⋆=z⋆𝟏⊤​z⋆.z^{\star}\in\arg\min_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{G}(v),\qquad\theta^{\star}=\frac{z^{\star}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}z^{\star}}. (3.3)

Thus z⋆z^{\star} gives the allocation per unit of budget that minimizes the largest target-specific variance, and θ⋆\theta^{\star} gives the corresponding fractions. For a fixed logger composition, Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta) is also the semiparametric efficiency bound discussed in Section 2.2, so this choice has the same fixed-design interpretation after accounting for the logger costs. We discuss the uniqueness of z⋆z^{\star} in Section 4.1.

The fixed-design variance (2.4) is finite under our bounded-reward assumption when the pooled probabilities are bounded away from zero on the target-policy supports, even if individual loggers are not. We measure this coverage by

κ⁡(θ)=ess​inf(x,a)∈𝒮⁡mθ​(a∣x).\kappa(\theta)=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}}m_{\theta}(a\mid x). (3.4)

When the contexts take finitely many values, for example finitely many subgroups, κ⁡(θ)\kappa(\theta) is a minimum of finitely many linear functions of θ\theta and can be computed exactly. For general context spaces, forced sampling can instead use a known lower bound on κ⁡(θ)\kappa(\theta), for example a finite minimum of nonnegative weighted sums of the θk\theta_{k} (Appendix A3.2). We impose this condition only at an optimal design.

Assumption 2.

There is a minimizer z⋆z^{\star} in (3.3) whose composition θ⋆\theta^{\star} satisfies κ⁡(θ⋆)≥κ⋆\kappa(\theta^{\star})\geq\kappa_{\star} for some κ⋆>0\kappa_{\star}>0.

This assumption allows individual loggers to assign zero probability to target-relevant actions, provided their mixture at the optimal design has sufficient coverage. Agarwal et al. (2017) note that their balanced estimator needs only that the average logging policy covers the target, and Kallus et al. (2021) distinguish this pooled overlap from the stronger requirement that every logger covers the target, which logger-specific weights need (He et al., 2019, see also). Per-logger lower bounds remain common in multi-logger evaluation (Lai et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023). If each logger is deployed with μk​(a∣x)≥μ0\mu_{k}(a\mid x)\geq\mu_{0} on 𝒮\mathcal{S} for a constant μ0>0\mu_{0}>0, as Agarwal et al. (2017) suggest for ensuring support, then mθ​(a∣x)=∑kθk​μk​(a∣x)≥μ0​∑kθk=μ0m_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\sum_{k}\theta_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x)\geq\mu_{0}\sum_{k}\theta_{k}=\mu_{0} for every composition θ\theta, so κ⁡(θ)≥μ0\kappa(\theta)\geq\mu_{0} and Assumption 2 holds with κ⋆=μ0\kappa_{\star}=\mu_{0}. Assumption 2 is a quantitative form of pooled overlap, imposed only at θ⋆\theta^{\star}, and individual loggers may give probability zero to actions that the targets use. Since θk⋆≤1\theta_{k}^{\star}\leq 1, it implies ∑kμk​(a∣x)≥κ⋆\sum_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x)\geq\kappa_{\star} on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, so the uniform mixture of the loggers also covers the targets.

3.2 Sequential Selection Rule

To choose the next logger, we compare the reduction in the worst-target variance GG that one more observation from each logger would bring, per unit of cost. Initially, we start with budget BB and no data. At time tt, the remaining budget is B−CtB-C_{t} and we choose the next logger from the set 𝒦t={k:ck≤B−Ct}.\mathcal{K}_{t}=\{k:c_{k}\leq B-C_{t}\}. Now, given the current allocation NtN_{t}, we want to purchase the next logger from 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t} that provides the largest reduction in GG. Therefore, for any count vector NN, define the reduction from purchasing one observation from logger kk by

Δk​(N)=G⁡(N)−G⁡(N+ek).\Delta_{k}(N)=G(N)-G(N+e_{k}). (3.5)

If the reward moments were known, the optimal allocation could be obtained by solving

minN∈ℤ+Kc⊤​N≤B⁡G⁡(N).\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{K}\\ c^{\top}N\leq B\end{subarray}}G(N). (3.6)

However, solving this integer optimization problem is computationally expensive for large budgets. Moreover, VjV_{j} and WjW_{j} are unknown in our setting. We therefore consider the simpler greedy rule

Kt+1greedy∈arg​maxk∈𝒦t⁡Δk​(Nt)ck,K_{t+1}^{\mathrm{greedy}}\in\argmax_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}\frac{\Delta_{k}(N_{t})}{c_{k}}, (3.7)

which chooses the affordable logger giving the largest immediate reduction in GG per unit cost.

The rule (3.7) cannot be used directly, for two reasons. First, the reductions are small and unknown. When the pooled coverage is bounded below, Gj​(Nt)G_{j}(N_{t}) is of order t−1t^{-1} while the target-specific reduction Δj,k​(Nt)=Gj​(Nt)−Gj​(Nt+ek)\Delta_{j,k}(N_{t})=G_{j}(N_{t})-G_{j}(N_{t}+e_{k}) is of order t−2t^{-2} (Appendix A2.2), so the reductions behave like derivatives of the criterion. They depend on the unknown VjV_{j} and WjW_{j}, and the rule must still rank them correctly across loggers. Second, GG is a maximum over targets. Its one-step change Δk​(N)\Delta_{k}(N) is not a combination of the target-specific changes, and GG is not smooth where the maximizing target switches.

We handle the second difficulty by replacing the maximum with a log-sum-exp approximation (Nesterov, 2005). This puts exponential weights on the target-specific reductions and introduces a bias of at most ρ​log⁡M\rho\log M, which vanishes as the smoothing parameter ρt\rho_{t} decreases. We handle the first by plugging estimates of the reward mean and variance into the closed form of the reductions. Our theory needs these estimates to be accurate on the t−2t^{-2} scale of the reductions, which is Assumption 4 in Section 4.1. The two fixes interact: as ρt\rho_{t} decreases, the weights become more sensitive to estimation error, so ρt\rho_{t} must decrease slowly relative to the estimation error (see Theorem 4.1).

Estimation.

Writing T=𝟏⊤​NT=\mathbf{1}^{\top}N, the target-specific reduction has the closed form (see Appendix A2.1 for derivation)

Δj,k​(N)=Gj​(N)−Gj​(N+ek)=𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)​μk​(a∣X)DN​(X,a)​{DN​(X,a)+μk​(a∣X)}+Vj(T+η0)​(T+1+η0).\Delta_{j,k}(N)=G_{j}(N)-G_{j}(N+e_{k})=\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{W_{j}(X,a)\mu_{k}(a\mid X)}{D_{N}(X,a)\{D_{N}(X,a)+\mu_{k}(a\mid X)\}}+\frac{V_{j}}{(T+\eta_{0})(T+1+\eta_{0})}. (3.8)

Let G^j,t\widehat{G}_{j,t} and Δ^j,k,t\widehat{\Delta}_{j,k,t} denote Gj​(Nt)G_{j}(N_{t}) and Δj,k​(Nt)\Delta_{j,k}(N_{t}) with VjV_{j} and WjW_{j} computed from estimates q^t\widehat{q}_{t} and σ^t2\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2} of the reward mean and variance, and with PXP_{X} replaced by the empirical distribution of the observed contexts (Appendix A3.4). Any regression estimators of the reward mean and variance can be used, and our experiments use ridge regression (Appendix A7.1). Lemma A3.11 gives conditions on these estimators under which Assumption 4 holds, and Corollary A3.1 verifies them for finite context spaces.

Smoothing.

To address the nonsmoothness of the worst-target criterion 𝒢⁡(v)=max1≤j≤M⁡𝒢j​(v)\mathcal{G}(v)=\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\mathcal{G}_{j}(v), we use a log-sum-exp approximation (Nesterov, 2005). For ρ>0\rho>0, define

Φρ​(v)=ρ​log⁡{∑j=1Mexp⁡(𝒢j​(v)/ρ)},𝒢⁡(v)≤Φρ​(v)≤𝒢⁡(v)+ρ​log⁡M.\Phi_{\rho}(v)=\rho\log\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp\bigl(\mathcal{G}_{j}(v)/\rho\bigr)\right\},\qquad\mathcal{G}(v)\leq\Phi_{\rho}(v)\leq\mathcal{G}(v)+\rho\log M. (3.9)

Hence Φρ​(v)→𝒢​(v)\Phi_{\rho}(v)\to\mathcal{G}(v) as ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0. Its gradient is ∇Φρ(v)=∑j=1Mωj(v;ρ)∇𝒢j(v)\nabla\Phi_{\rho}(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\omega_{j}(v;\rho)\nabla\mathcal{G}_{j}(v), with exponential weights ωj​(v,ρ)=exp⁡{𝒢j​(v)/ρ}/∑ℓ=1Mexp⁡{𝒢ℓ​(v)/ρ}.\omega_{j}(v;\rho)=\exp\{\mathcal{G}_{j}(v)/\rho\}/\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\exp\{\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(v)/\rho\}. Therefore, policies with larger values of 𝒢j​(v)\mathcal{G}_{j}(v) receive larger weights. We now relate the gradient to the one-step gains. Recall that CN​Gj​(N)≈𝒢j​(zN)C_{N}G_{j}(N)\approx\mathcal{G}_{j}(z_{N}) for large budgets. Hence, we have CN2Δj,k(N)≈−∂k𝒢j(zN)C_{N}^{2}\Delta_{j,k}(N)\approx-\partial_{k}\mathcal{G}_{j}(z_{N}). Using the expression for ∇Φρ\nabla\Phi_{\rho}, this gives

−⟨∇Φρ​(zN),ekck⟩≈CN2ck​∑j=1Mωj​(zN,ρ)​Δj,k​(N).-\left\langle\nabla\Phi_{\rho}(z_{N}),\frac{e_{k}}{c_{k}}\right\rangle\approx\frac{C_{N}^{2}}{c_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\omega_{j}(z_{N};\rho)\Delta_{j,k}(N).

Since CN2C_{N}^{2} is common to all loggers, this motivates using the weighted gains for selecting the next logger. Lemmas A3.8 and A3.9 make this idea precise. So that the bias ρt​log⁡M\rho_{t}\log M vanishes, we let the smoothing parameter decrease with expenditure, ρt=ρ0​Ct−α\rho_{t}=\rho_{0}C_{t}^{-\alpha} with ρ0>0\rho_{0}>0 and 0<α<10<\alpha<1, and estimate the weights by ω^j,t=exp⁡(Ct​G^j,t/ρt)/∑ℓ=1Mexp⁡(Ct​G^ℓ,t/ρt).\widehat{\omega}_{j,t}=\exp(C_{t}\widehat{G}_{j,t}/\rho_{t})/\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\exp(C_{t}\widehat{G}_{\ell,t}/\rho_{t}). The weights therefore become increasingly concentrated on the policies with the largest estimated criterion values. We define the acquisition index for logger kk as

S^t,k=1ck​∑j=1Mω^j,t​Δ^j,k,t.\widehat{S}_{t,k}=\frac{1}{c_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\widehat{\omega}_{j,t}\widehat{\Delta}_{j,k,t}. (3.10)

The rule selects the affordable logger with the largest index. In our experiments we use ρ0=0.5\rho_{0}=0.5 and α=0.4\alpha=0.4. Sensitivity to these choices is reported in Appendix A7.5. The additional condition on α\alpha needed for the convergence result is given in Section 4.1.

3.3 Algorithm

In this section we state our final algorithm. Combining the previous subsections, the main rule is to select the affordable logger kk at step tt with the largest index S^t,k\widehat{S}_{t,k} except certain times as stated below. The full procedure is stated in Algorithm 1. The initialization gives each logger a small number of observations before selection begins. The refit interval mm avoids refitting the nuisance models after every acquisition.

Forced sampling.

Although Assumption 2 controls coverage once the algorithm is near the optimal allocation, it does not control coverage early in the acquisition. If the early estimates undervalue the loggers that cover some target actions, the rule may rarely purchase from them, and the estimates for those actions are then slow to improve. Forced sampling of under-sampled arms or strata is a standard remedy in adaptive allocation (Antos et al., 2010; Étoré and Jourdain, 2010; Garivier and Kaufmann, 2016), and adaptive designs often keep assignment probabilities above a floor that vanishes over time (Hadad et al., 2021; Bibaut et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2023). We use forced sampling of this kind, acting on pooled coverage.

Recall that κ⁡(θ)\kappa(\theta) is the essential infimum of mθ​(a∣x)m_{\theta}(a\mid x) over the context-action pairs used by at least one target policy. If κ⁡(θt)\kappa(\theta_{t}) falls below a threshold χt\chi_{t} that vanishes over time, the algorithm purchases an observation from the logger with the smallest count. Otherwise, it selects the logger using the usual greedy rule. We take

χt=χ0​t−υ,0<υ<1,\chi_{t}=\chi_{0}t^{-\upsilon},\qquad 0<\upsilon<1,

where 0<χ0≤κ⁡(𝟏/K)8.0<\chi_{0}\leq\frac{\kappa(\mathbf{1}/K)}{8}. Our convergence results require

0<α<1,0<υ<1−α4,0<χ0≤κ⁡(𝟏/K)8,n0K≥4.0<\alpha<1,\qquad 0<\upsilon<\frac{1-\alpha}{4},\qquad 0<\chi_{0}\leq\frac{\kappa(\mathbf{1}/K)}{8},\qquad\frac{n_{0}}{K}\geq 4. (3.11)

Lemma A3.4 shows that forced sampling maintains κ⁡(θt)≥χt/2\kappa(\theta_{t})\geq\chi_{t}/2 while all loggers are affordable. It also shows that the number of forced purchases up to time tt is O⁡(t1−υ)O(t^{1-\upsilon}). Under the conditions of Theorem 4.1, the allocation converges to θ⋆\theta^{\star} and forced sampling eventually stops.

If forced sampling uses a lower bound κ~≤κ\widetilde{\kappa}\leq\kappa in place of κ\kappa, the same guarantees hold under the conditions given in Appendix A3.2.

Final estimation.

When acquisition ends, we estimate JJ using the entire acquired sample and the realized logger composition θ^B=NTB/TB\widehat{\theta}_{B}=N_{T_{B}}/T_{B}. The final pooled estimator replaces qq in (2.3) by a reward regression q^B\widehat{q}_{B} fitted on that sample, truncated to [−Rmax,Rmax][-R_{\max},R_{\max}]:

J^B,j=1TB∑i=1TB[q^B,j(Xi)+πj​(Ai∣Xi)mθ^B​(Ai∣Xi){Ri−q^B(Xi,Ai)}],j=1,…,M,\widehat{J}_{B,j}=\frac{1}{T_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{B}}\left[\widehat{q}_{B,j}(X_{i})+\frac{\pi_{j}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{m_{\widehat{\theta}_{B}}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}\{R_{i}-\widehat{q}_{B}(X_{i},A_{i})\}\right],\qquad j=1,\ldots,M, (3.12)

where q^B,j​(x)=∑a∈𝒜πj​(a∣x)​q^B​(x,a)\widehat{q}_{B,j}(x)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{j}(a\mid x)\widehat{q}_{B}(x,a). Unlike the fixed-design setting, the final logger composition θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} is random and depends on the adaptive selection process. We study its effect on inference in Section 4.2.

4 Theory

We divide this section into two subsections. We first prove that Adaptive Greedy actually converges to the optimal minimax design under mild assumptions in Section 4.1. We then establish the asymptotic normality of our estimator in Section 4.2. All proofs are in Appendices A3, A4, and A6.

4.1 Convergence and Asymptotics

In Section 3, we defined z⋆z^{\star} (equation (3.3)) which minimizes the criterion 𝒢\mathcal{G}. In this subsection, we are interested in two questions. First is when z⋆z^{\star} is unique and if it is, whether zTBz_{T_{B}} converges to z⋆z^{\star} as BB increases. The second is the rate. Theorem 4.1 answers both.

The main idea is that choosing the logger with the largest gain per unit cost amounts to choosing the vertex ek/cke_{k}/c_{k} of 𝒞\mathcal{C} that minimizes the linear approximation of the criterion at ztz_{t}. When the algorithm purchases one observation from logger kk, zt=Nt/Ctz_{t}=N_{t}/C_{t} changes according to

zt+1=(1−γt)​zt+γt​ekck,γt=ckCt+ck,z_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_{t})z_{t}+\gamma_{t}\frac{e_{k}}{c_{k}},\qquad\gamma_{t}=\frac{c_{k}}{C_{t}+c_{k}}, (4.1)

so the purchase moves ztz_{t} toward that vertex by the step γt\gamma_{t}. This is similar to the Frank–Wolfe, or conditional-gradient, method (Frank and Wolfe, 1956; Jaggi, 2013), used in optimal design by Fedorov (1972) and Wynn (1970). Such steps converge to the minimizer of a smooth convex function when their lengths tend to zero and their sum diverges, as γt\gamma_{t}, being of order Ct−1C_{t}^{-1}, does.

Strong convexity of 𝒢\mathcal{G} serves two purposes. If 𝒢\mathcal{G} is mm-strongly convex, its minimizer z⋆z^{\star} is unique and 𝒢⁡(z)−𝒢⁡(z⋆)≥m2​‖z−z⋆‖22\mathcal{G}(z)-\mathcal{G}(z^{\star})\geq\tfrac{m}{2}\|z-z^{\star}\|_{2}^{2} for every z∈𝒞z\in\mathcal{C}, so convergence of 𝒢⁡(zt)\mathcal{G}(z_{t}) to 𝒢⁡(z⋆)\mathcal{G}(z^{\star}) forces ztz_{t} to converge to z⋆z^{\star}. Recall that a function ff on 𝒞\mathcal{C} is mm-strongly convex if f⁡(z)−m2​‖z‖22f(z)-\tfrac{m}{2}\|z\|_{2}^{2} is convex; for twice differentiable ff this holds exactly when, along every segment in 𝒞\mathcal{C} with direction hh, the second derivative of ff is at least m​‖h‖22m\|h\|_{2}^{2}. Any feasible direction hh satisfies c⊤​h=0c^{\top}h=0, and on such directions h⊤​∇2𝒢j​(z)​h≥2​cmin3​h⊤​Qj​hh^{\top}\nabla^{2}\mathcal{G}_{j}(z)h\geq 2c_{\min}^{3}h^{\top}Q_{j}h (see the proof of Proposition A3.2 in Appendix A6), where

Qj=Vj​𝟏𝟏⊤+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)​𝝁​(X,a)​𝝁​(X,a)⊤.Q_{j}=V_{j}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}W_{j}(X,a)\bm{\mu}(X,a)\bm{\mu}(X,a)^{\top}. (4.2)

We therefore impose the following condition.

Assumption 3.

For every target policy πj\pi_{j}, λj=infh≠0,c⊤​h=0h⊤​Qj​h‖h‖22>0.\lambda_{j}=\inf_{h\neq 0,\ c^{\top}h=0}\frac{h^{\top}Q_{j}h}{\|h\|_{2}^{2}}>0.

This assumption ensures sufficient curvature of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which guarantees uniqueness of z⋆z^{\star}. The condition plays the role of the full-rank conditions of optimal design (Pukelsheim, 2006). Under Assumptions 1, 2, and 3, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly convex with m=2​cmin3​minj​λjm=2c_{\min}^{3}\min_{j}\lambda_{j}, and thus, z⋆z^{\star} is unique. These results are Proposition A3.2 and Lemma A3.2 in Appendix A3, and their proofs are in Appendix A6.

Now, we focus on the rate of convergence. Recall that our selection rule uses G^j,t\widehat{G}_{j,t} and Δ^j,k,t\widehat{\Delta}_{j,k,t} from Section 3.2. Since Gj​(Nt)G_{j}(N_{t}) is of order Ct−1C_{t}^{-1} and Δj,k​(Nt)\Delta_{j,k}(N_{t}) is of order Ct−2C_{t}^{-2} when pooled coverage is bounded below, we need their estimation errors to be small on these scales. We impose the following assumption.

Assumption 4.

There is a deterministic sequence rt→0r_{t}\to 0 such that, almost surely for all sufficiently large tt,

Ct​maxj​|G^j,t−Gj​(Nt)|≤rt,Ct2​maxj,k​|Δ^j,k,t−Δj,k​(Nt)|≤rt.C_{t}\max_{j}\left|\widehat{G}_{j,t}-G_{j}(N_{t})\right|\leq r_{t},\qquad C_{t}^{2}\max_{j,k}\left|\widehat{\Delta}_{j,k,t}-\Delta_{j,k}(N_{t})\right|\leq r_{t}. (4.3)

The accuracy of these estimates depends on the estimation of VjV_{j}, WjW_{j}, and PXP_{X}. Lemma A3.11 in Appendix A3 gives sufficient conditions for Assumption 4. We also verify these conditions for finite context spaces in Corollary A3.1.

We now make the Frank–Wolfe interpretation more precise. Write zt=zNtz_{t}=z_{N_{t}}, and recall from Section 3.2 that the rescaled index Ct2​S^t,kC_{t}^{2}\widehat{S}_{t,k} is approximately −⟨∇Φρt​(zt),ek/ck⟩-\langle\nabla\Phi_{\rho_{t}}(z_{t}),e_{k}/c_{k}\rangle.

Proposition 4.1.

Under Assumptions 1 and 4, there is a finite constant DD, depending only on cminc_{\min}, cmaxc_{\max}, RmaxR_{\max}, η\eta, η0\eta_{0}, and ρ0\rho_{0}, such that, almost surely for all sufficiently large tt,

max1≤k≤K⁡|Ct2​S^t,k+⟨∇Φρt​(zt),ekck⟩|≤εt,εt=D⁡{κ​(θt)−2​Ctα​rt+κ​(θt)−4​Ctα−1}.\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\Big|C_{t}^{2}\widehat{S}_{t,k}+\Big\langle\nabla\Phi_{\rho_{t}}(z_{t}),\frac{e_{k}}{c_{k}}\Big\rangle\Big|\leq\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}=D\big\{\kappa(\theta_{t})^{-2}C_{t}^{\alpha}r_{t}+\kappa(\theta_{t})^{-4}C_{t}^{\alpha-1}\big\}. (4.4)

Consequently, whenever all loggers are affordable and the step is not forced, the vertex vt=eKt+1/cKt+1v_{t}=e_{K_{t+1}}/c_{K_{t+1}} purchased by Algorithm 1 satisfies

⟨∇Φρt​(zt),vt⟩≤minv∈𝒞⁡⟨∇Φρt​(zt),v⟩+δt,δt=2​εt.\langle\nabla\Phi_{\rho_{t}}(z_{t}),v_{t}\rangle\leq\min_{v\in\mathcal{C}}\langle\nabla\Phi_{\rho_{t}}(z_{t}),v\rangle+\delta_{t},\qquad\delta_{t}=2\varepsilon_{t}. (4.5)

This proposition formalizes the connection between our selection rule and the Frank–Wolfe method. Our algorithm chooses the logger with the largest estimated index S^t,k\widehat{S}_{t,k} while a Frank–Wolfe step would minimize the linear approximation of Φρt\Phi_{\rho_{t}} over 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The first bound shows that these two are close and the second shows that our selection is a δt\delta_{t}-approximate conditional-gradient step. Note that the approximation error depends on both rtr_{t} and pooled coverage κ⁡(θt)\kappa(\theta_{t}). Therefore, if coverage is small, the errors can become fairly large. As discussed in Section 3.3, forced sampling is introduced to prevent exactly this. Lemma A3.4 in Appendix A3 shows that κ⁡(θt)≥χt/2\kappa(\theta_{t})\geq\chi_{t}/2 and that the step sizes of the forced purchases are summable. Together with the accuracy assumption, these bounds allow us to establish convergence of the acquired allocation.

We now state our main result. Because the last purchases depend on the budget, we state the estimation condition along a single sequence that does not depend on BB: the infinite-budget sequence, in which every logger remains affordable, with counts N¯t\bar{N}_{t} and expenditure C¯t\bar{C}_{t}. The relation between the budget-BB and infinite-budget sequences is provided in Appendix A3. The conditions in the theorem are needed to control the errors in Proposition 4.1. Recall that υ\upsilon determines how quickly the forced-sampling threshold decreases. The condition υ<(1−α)/4\upsilon<(1-\alpha)/4 in (3.11) ensures that the error terms involving the pooled coverage decrease as more observations are collected. We also require tα+2​υ​rt→0t^{\alpha+2\upsilon}r_{t}\to 0 to control the error from estimating the criterion and gains.

Theorem 4.1.

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, and 3 hold, Assumption 4 holds along the infinite-budget sequence, with NtN_{t} and CtC_{t} replaced by N¯t\bar{N}_{t} and C¯t\bar{C}_{t}, the tuning constants satisfy (3.11), and tα+2​υ​rt→0t^{\alpha+2\upsilon}r_{t}\to 0. Then

  1. (i)

    zTB→z⋆z_{T_{B}}\to z^{\star} and θ^B→θ⋆\widehat{\theta}_{B}\to\theta^{\star} almost surely as B→∞B\to\infty, and forced sampling occurs only finitely often along the infinite-budget sequence.

  2. (ii)

    If, moreover, rt=O⁡(t−βr)r_{t}=O(t^{-\beta_{r}}) for some βr>α\beta_{r}>\alpha, then almost surely

    𝒢(zTB)−𝒢(z⋆)=O(B−β),∥θ^B−θ⋆∥2=O(B−β/2),\mathcal{G}(z_{T_{B}})-\mathcal{G}(z^{\star})=O(B^{-\beta}),\qquad\|\widehat{\theta}_{B}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}=O(B^{-\beta/2}),

    where β=min⁡{α,1−α,βr−α}\beta=\min\{\alpha,1-\alpha,\beta_{r}-\alpha\}.

Part (i) shows that Adaptive Greedy indeed converges to the optimal design z⋆z^{\star}. It also shows that forced sampling eventually stops once the allocation is sufficiently close to the optimum as the coverage is bounded away from zero and the usual greedy rule takes over. In part (ii) each term of β\beta comes from one source of error: smoothing gives α\alpha, purchasing one observation at a time gives 1−α1-\alpha, and estimation gives βr−α\beta_{r}-\alpha. The first term increases in α\alpha and the other two decrease, so taking α=min⁡{βr,1}/2\alpha=\min\{\beta_{r},1\}/2 gives the largest exponent, β=min⁡{βr,1}/2\beta=\min\{\beta_{r},1\}/2.

4.2 Inference

In this subsection we derive the asymptotic normality of J^B\widehat{J}_{B}. The main difficulty is that, unlike in the fixed-design setting, where the estimator is simply an average of independent terms with variance Aj​(θ)/tA_{j}(\theta)/t, each observation in (3.12) is divided by the pooled behavior probability mθ^Bm_{\widehat{\theta}_{B}} and θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} depends on the rewards observed during purchasing. The denominator is therefore unknown when each observation is collected. Nevertheless, we show that the estimator is asymptotically normal and that its asymptotic variance for target πj\pi_{j} is Aj​(θ⋆)A_{j}(\theta^{\star}), the fixed-design bound at the composition to which the rule converges.

We compare J^B\widehat{J}_{B} with averages in which qq replaces q^B\widehat{q}_{B} and a fixed composition θ\theta with κ⁡(θ)>0\kappa(\theta)>0 replaces θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B}; their summand is the score

ψi​(θ)=qΠ​(Xi)+π⁡(Ai∣Xi)mθ​(Ai∣Xi)​{Ri−q⁡(Xi,Ai)},\psi_{i}(\theta)=q_{\Pi}(X_{i})+\frac{\pi(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{m_{\theta}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}\{R_{i}-q(X_{i},A_{i})\}, (4.6)

where π⁡(a∣x)={π1​(a∣x),…,πM​(a∣x)}⊤\pi(a\mid x)=\{\pi_{1}(a\mid x),\ldots,\pi_{M}(a\mid x)\}^{\top} and qΠ​(x)={q1​(x),…,qM​(x)}⊤q_{\Pi}(x)=\{q_{1}(x),\ldots,q_{M}(x)\}^{\top}.

The main idea involves three steps. First, consider J~B⋆=1TB​∑i=1TBψi​(θ⋆)\widetilde{J}_{B}^{\star}=\frac{1}{T_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{B}}\psi_{i}(\theta^{\star}) which uses the limiting composition θ⋆\theta^{\star}, which is unknown. Although the loggers are selected adaptively, KiK_{i} is chosen before observation ii is collected and since Ri−q⁡(Xi,Ai)R_{i}-q(X_{i},A_{i}) has conditional mean zero, ψi​(θ⋆)−J\psi_{i}(\theta^{\star})-J also has conditional mean zero given the past. Thus, these scores form a martingale difference sequence. Their average conditional variance depends on θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B}, which converges to θ⋆\theta^{\star} by Theorem 4.1. The limiting variance is therefore ΣA​(θ⋆)\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star}), where

ΣA​(θ)=Cov⁡{qΠ​(X)}+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜σ2​(X,a)​π​(a∣X)​π​(a∣X)⊤mθ​(a∣X),\Sigma_{A}(\theta)=\mathrm{Cov}\{q_{\Pi}(X)\}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\sigma^{2}(X,a)\pi(a\mid X)\pi(a\mid X)^{\top}}{m_{\theta}(a\mid X)}, (4.7)

and the jjth diagonal entry of ΣA​(θ)\Sigma_{A}(\theta) is Aj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta) in (2.5). We can then apply a martingale central limit theorem (Hall and Heyde, 1980). The second step is to replace θ⋆\theta^{\star} by θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B}. By Assumption 2, the pooled probabilities remain bounded away from zero when the composition is sufficiently close to θ⋆\theta^{\star}. Since θ^B→θ⋆\widehat{\theta}_{B}\to\theta^{\star}, we need to show that using θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} instead of θ⋆\theta^{\star} does not change the limiting distribution. We show in Appendix A4 that

1TB∑i=1TB{ψi(θ^B)−ψi(θ⋆)}=op(TB−1/2).\frac{1}{T_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{B}}\{\psi_{i}(\widehat{\theta}_{B})-\psi_{i}(\theta^{\star})\}=o_{p}(T_{B}^{-1/2}).

Finally, we need to account for the estimated reward regression q^B\widehat{q}_{B}. Replacing qq by q^B\widehat{q}_{B} introduces the remainder

ℛB,j​(θ)=1TB​∑i=1TB[{q^B,j−qj}​(Xi)−πj​(Ai∣Xi)mθ​(Ai∣Xi)​{q^B−q}​(Xi,Ai)].\mathcal{R}_{B,j}(\theta)=\frac{1}{T_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{B}}\left[\{\widehat{q}_{B,j}-q_{j}\}(X_{i})-\frac{\pi_{j}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{m_{\theta}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}\{\widehat{q}_{B}-q\}(X_{i},A_{i})\right]. (4.8)

We therefore impose the following assumption.

Assumption 5.

There is a deterministic sequence rB↓0r_{B}\downarrow 0 such that

ℙ(∥θ^B−θ⋆∥2≤rB)→1,max1≤j≤Msup‖θ−θ⋆‖2≤rB|ℛB,j(θ)|=op(TB−1/2).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\|\widehat{\theta}_{B}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\leq r_{B}\right)\to 1,\qquad\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\leq r_{B}}|\mathcal{R}_{B,j}(\theta)|=o_{p}(T_{B}^{-1/2}). (4.9)

This is the usual condition under which the estimated regression does not affect an augmented estimator at first order, and in semiparametric inference it is commonly obtained by sample splitting or cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). In Appendix A5 we describe a block-split estimator, motivated by cross-fitting, that avoids reusing the same observations for regression. Related conditions for adaptively collected data appear in Hadad et al. (2021), Zhan et al. (2021), and Bibaut et al. (2021). Because θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} is random, the remainder is required to be small over a neighborhood of θ⋆\theta^{\star} that contains θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} with probability tending to one. Since rB→0r_{B}\to 0, this neighborhood eventually lies in {θ:‖θ−θ⋆‖1≤κ⋆/2}\{\theta:\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|_{1}\leq\kappa_{\star}/2\}, where mθ≥κ⋆/2m_{\theta}\geq\kappa_{\star}/2 on 𝒮\mathcal{S} by Assumption 2, so the remainder is well defined there. The first condition in (4.9) only limits how fast this neighborhood may shrink, and by Theorem 4.1 it holds for any rBr_{B} that decreases slowly enough. The assumption concerns only the final regression in (3.12) and is separate from Assumption 4, which governs the estimates used while purchasing.

Theorem 4.2.

Under the conditions of part (i) of Theorem 4.1 and Assumption 5,

TB​(J^B−J)→N⁡{0,ΣA​(θ⋆)}in distribution.\sqrt{T_{B}}\left(\widehat{J}_{B}-J\right)\to N\{0,\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star})\}\qquad\text{in distribution.} (4.10)

For each target, the asymptotic variance of the estimate computed from the purchased sample is therefore Aj​(θ⋆)A_{j}(\theta^{\star}), the fixed-design bound at the composition to which the rule converges, which is the quantity whose largest value over Π\Pi the rule was built to reduce.

We need to estimate the covariance as well. With ψ^i\widehat{\psi}_{i} the MM-vector summand of (3.12), we use

Σ^B=1TB​∑i=1TB(ψ^i−J^B)​(ψ^i−J^B)⊤.\widehat{\Sigma}_{B}=\frac{1}{T_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{B}}(\widehat{\psi}_{i}-\widehat{J}_{B})(\widehat{\psi}_{i}-\widehat{J}_{B})^{\top}. (4.11)
Corollary 4.1.

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 4.2 hold and the terminal regression is consistent in mean square over the sample, TB−1​∑i≤TB∑a∈𝒜{q^B​(Xi,a)−q⁡(Xi,a)}2→0T_{B}^{-1}\sum_{i\leq T_{B}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\{\widehat{q}_{B}(X_{i},a)-q(X_{i},a)\}^{2}\to 0 in probability. Then Σ^B→ΣA​(θ⋆)\widehat{\Sigma}_{B}\to\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star}) in probability. Consequently, for every target πj\pi_{j} with Aj​(θ⋆)>0A_{j}(\theta^{\star})>0, the intervals

J^B,j±z1−γ/2​(Σ^B)j​j/TB,j=1,…,M,\widehat{J}_{B,j}\pm z_{1-\gamma/2}\sqrt{(\widehat{\Sigma}_{B})_{jj}/T_{B}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,M, (4.12)

have asymptotic coverage 1−γ1-\gamma for JjJ_{j}.

Because Theorem 4.2 is a joint statement over the target class, simultaneous regions also follow. A Bonferroni band replaces z1−γ/2z_{1-\gamma/2} in (4.12) by z1−γ/(2​M)z_{1-\gamma/(2M)}, and a less conservative band uses the 1−γ1-\gamma quantile of maxj⁡|Zj|\max_{j}|Z_{j}|, where Z∼N⁡(0,R^B)Z\sim N(0,\widehat{R}_{B}) and R^B\widehat{R}_{B} is the correlation matrix associated with Σ^B\widehat{\Sigma}_{B}.

The pooled weighting also matters for efficiency. A logger-specific estimator, which divides each observation by the propensity of the logger that generated it, has fixed-design covariance ΣL​(θ)\Sigma_{L}(\theta), defined in (A4.9) of Appendix A4.4, and

ΣA​(θ)⪯ΣL​(θ)for every ​θ∈𝒮K,\Sigma_{A}(\theta)\preceq\Sigma_{L}(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{K}, (4.13)

an ordering known for fixed designs (Agarwal et al., 2017; Kallus et al., 2021), where the right side is infinite when a logger with θk>0\theta_{k}>0 gives probability zero to an action that a target policy uses. Theorem 4.2 shows that the pooled estimator variance Aj​(θ⋆)A_{j}(\theta^{\star}) is no larger than the fixed-design variance of the logger-specific estimator at the same composition.

5 Numerical Studies

In this section, we evaluate Adaptive Greedy (Algorithm 1) in three synthetic environments with known optimal designs and in a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 (Hammer et al., 1996a; Hammer et al., 1996b). Implementation details, the complete data-generating process, and additional experiments are given in Appendix A7.

5.1 Simulation Setup

All three environments have K=5K=5 loggers, five actions, M=4M=4 target policies, and a five-dimensional context drawn from a three-component Gaussian mixture. The reward is a clipped normal variable,

R=min{4,max(−4,R∘)},R∘∣X=x,A=a∼N{q0(x,a),s2(x,a)},R=\min\{4,\max(-4,R^{\circ})\},\qquad R^{\circ}\mid X=x,A=a\sim N\{q_{0}(x,a),s^{2}(x,a)\},

where q0​(x,a)q_{0}(x,a) is linear in xx, with an additional interaction x1​x2x_{1}x_{2} for actions 3 to 5, and the variance s2​(x,a)s^{2}(x,a) is larger for actions 4 and 5 and increases with x32x_{3}^{2}. Loggers 1 to 4 concentrate on the action pairs (1,2)(1,2), (2,3)(2,3), (3,4)(3,4), and (4,5)(4,5), so each covers a different part of the action space, while Logger 5 is close to uniform. The target policies are softmax policies mixed with a uniform exploration floor. The environments differ as follows.

  • •

    Environment A has costs c=(1,2,4,8,16)c=(1,2,4,8,16) and optimal design θ⋆≈(0.784,0,0.085,0.132,0)\theta^{\star}\approx(0.784,0,0.085,0.132,0).

  • •

    Environment B keeps the loggers and costs of Environment A but uses more concentrated target policies. Its optimal design θ⋆≈(0.715,0.074,0.138,0.073,0)\theta^{\star}\approx(0.715,0.074,0.138,0.073,0) includes Logger 2, so a change in the targets alone changes which loggers are worth purchasing from.

  • •

    Environment C keeps the policies of Environment A and changes the costs to c=(1,4,16,8,2)c=(1,4,16,8,2). Its optimal design θ⋆≈(0.257,0,0,0,0.743)\theta^{\star}\approx(0.257,0,0,0,0.743) puts most of the sample on Logger 5 even though Logger 1 is cheaper, so the best allocation depends on statistical value per unit cost rather than on cost alone.

We compare Adaptive Greedy with five procedures. All of them use the same initialization and, where they need them, the same estimators of the reward mean and variance.

  • •

    Reoptimized plug-in re-estimates VjV_{j} and WjW_{j} every ten observations, solves a continuous relaxation of the static allocation problem (3.6) with these estimates, rounds the resulting allocation to integer counts, and purchases toward that allocation until the next update.

  • •

    Estimated static solves the same relaxed problem once, after the initialization, and follows the resulting integer allocation to the end.

  • •

    Oracle static uses the same procedure with the true VjV_{j} and WjW_{j}. It is not feasible in practice and serves as a reference.

  • •

    Equal expenditure spends the same amount on each logger, so its sample fractions are proportional to 1/ck1/c_{k}.

  • •

    Cheapest only always purchases from the cheapest affordable logger.

Every procedure starts with four observations from each logger. For each action, we estimate the reward mean by ridge regression and the reward variance from the squared residuals of that fit (Appendix A7.1). Both are refitted every ten observations. Adaptive Greedy uses α=0.4\alpha=0.4 and ρ0=0.5\rho_{0}=0.5 in all settings, and forced sampling uses χ0=10−4\chi_{0}=10^{-4} and υ=0.01\upsilon=0.01. Every logger in our experiments gives every action a probability bounded below by more than χ0\chi_{0}, so forced sampling never occurs (Appendix A7.1). After the budget is spent, the policy values are estimated by the final estimator (3.12). Since the design criterion is a worst case over the target class, our main accuracy measure is the worst-target root mean squared error,

WorstRMSE=max1≤j≤M⁡{1R​∑r=1R(J^r,j−Jj)2}1/2,\operatorname{WorstRMSE}=\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\Big\{\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\widehat{J}_{r,j}-J_{j})^{2}\Big\}^{1/2},

where J^r,j\widehat{J}_{r,j} is the estimate of JjJ_{j} in replication rr. To measure how close the purchased design z^=zTB\widehat{z}=z_{T_{B}} is to the optimal design, we also report ‖θ^−θ⋆‖2\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2} and 𝒢⁡(z^)/𝒢⁡(z⋆)\mathcal{G}(\widehat{z})/\mathcal{G}(z^{\star}), which equals one at the optimal design. The budgets are B∈{500,1000,1500,3000,6000,12000,24000}B\in\{500,1000,1500,3000,6000,12000,24000\}, with R=200R=200 replications in Environments A and B and R=100R=100 in Environment C. We use common random numbers across procedures. For RMSE quantities, one Monte Carlo standard error is computed from 50005000 bootstrap resamples of the replications. For quantities averaged directly over replications, such as 𝒢⁡(z^)/𝒢⁡(z⋆)\mathcal{G}(\widehat{z})/\mathcal{G}(z^{\star}) and ‖θ^−θ⋆‖2\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}, it is the sample standard deviation divided by R\sqrt{R}.

5.2 Simulation Results

Figure 1 and Table 1 show that Adaptive Greedy is among the most accurate feasible procedures in all three environments. Its accuracy also approaches that of Oracle static as the budget grows. At B=24000B=24000, its worst-target RMSE is within about 2%2\% of Oracle static in every environment. It is 17%17\% and 22%22\% lower than that of Estimated static in Environments A and B, 15%15\% to 21%21\% lower than that of Equal expenditure, and 42%42\% to 51%51\% lower than that of Cheapest only. Reoptimized plug-in reaches almost the same accuracy as Adaptive Greedy. In Environment C, Estimated static also performs well, while Cheapest only has about twice the worst-target RMSE of Adaptive Greedy, which confirms that cost alone does not identify a good design. At small budgets, the differences between procedures are smaller and their ordering varies. Paired bootstrap comparisons separate Adaptive Greedy from Cheapest only at every budget, and from Estimated static and Equal expenditure at most budgets in Environments A and B (Appendix A7.4).

Figure 2 shows that the design purchased by Adaptive Greedy converges to the optimal design in all three environments, as parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem 4.1 predict. Both 𝒢⁡(z^)/𝒢⁡(z⋆)\mathcal{G}(\widehat{z})/\mathcal{G}(z^{\star}) and ‖θ^−θ⋆‖2\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2} decrease steadily with the budget.

The Wald intervals of Corollary 4.1 are well calibrated. We use R=500R=500 replications in Environments A and B at B=6000B=6000 and B=24000B=24000. The ratio of the mean estimated standard error to the empirical standard deviation lies between 0.9890.989 and 1.0601.060. Target-specific 95%95\% coverage lies between 0.9440.944 and 0.9660.966, and simultaneous coverage lies between 0.9500.950 and 0.9600.960 (Appendix A7.6). The appendix reports three further findings. First, Adaptive Greedy is robust to a misleading initialization, which degrades Estimated static much more (Appendix A7.5). Second, its accuracy changes little over a range of α\alpha and ρ0\rho_{0} (Appendix A7.5). Finally, the design criterion closely tracks estimation accuracy, with a correlation of about 0.970.97 at budgets of at least 30003000 (Appendix A7.4).

5.3 Comparison with Reoptimized Plug-in

Adaptive Greedy and Reoptimized plug-in reach similar accuracy when the budget is spent, but they get there differently. Reoptimized plug-in plans for the declared budget BB. However, Adaptive Greedy uses BB only to decide when to stop, so its purchases up to any point do not depend on BB. This matters when the final budget is uncertain or the run may end early. In Environment A, we ran both procedures with budget 50005000 and recorded their designs at intermediate budgets. We also ran separate runs whose budget equals each intermediate budget. Figure 3 shows that the Adaptive Greedy design at every intermediate budget is almost the same as that of a run planned for that budget, so stopping early costs little. The Reoptimized plug-in design instead moves away from the optimum early on, with 𝒢⁡(z^)/𝒢⁡(z⋆)\mathcal{G}(\widehat{z})/\mathcal{G}(z^{\star}) rising from 1.411.41 at B=500B=500 to 1.721.72 at B=1000B=1000, because its early purchases follow a plan made for B=5000B=5000 (Appendix A7.7).

Adaptive Greedy is also much cheaper to run, since it compares KK indices at each step instead of solving an allocation problem every ten observations. In Environment A, Reoptimized plug-in took 8.78.7 times as long as Adaptive Greedy at B=12000B=12000 (64236423 versus 742742 seconds) and 9.49.4 times as long at B=24000B=24000 (1644216442 versus 17501750 seconds). Thus Adaptive Greedy matches the accuracy of repeated reoptimization at about a tenth of its computing cost, and it provides a good design at any stopping point.

5.4 Application to ACTG 175 Data

The AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 (Hammer et al., 1996a) was a randomized trial in HIV-infected adults that compared four treatments, zidovudine (ZDV), ZDV with didanosine (ddI), ZDV with zalcitabine, and ddI alone. The public data (Hammer et al., 1996b) contain 21392139 subjects with complete records and have been used to study individualized treatment regimes (Fan et al., 2017). We take the four treatments as the actions, seven baseline covariates as the context (age, weight, CD4 count, CD8 count, Karnofsky score, symptomatic status, and prior antiretroviral therapy), and the change in CD4 count from baseline to around week 2020, divided by 100100, as the reward. To make the policy values and the optimal design known, we fit an arm-specific regression of the reward on the covariates and generate rewards from it, with contexts resampled from the 21392139 subjects (Appendix A7.8).

We construct five loggers with costs c=(1,2,4,3,8)c=(1,2,4,3,8). Loggers 1 to 4 each favor a different pair of treatments, and Logger 5 is uniform. The loggers and costs are part of the experimental design and do not describe the trial itself. Of the four target policies, one favors the treatments with higher fitted rewards and three are softmax policies. The optimal design θ⋆≈(0.811,0,0.028,0.161,0)\theta^{\star}\approx(0.811,0,0.028,0.161,0) uses only Loggers 1, 3, and 4. Logger 1 covers the first two treatments cheaply, Loggers 3 and 4 cover the other two, and the broad coverage of the uniform logger does not justify its cost. We use budgets 500500, 15001500, 60006000, and 1200012000, with R=200R=200 replications at each.

Table 2 shows the same pattern as the simulations. At B=12000B=12000, Adaptive Greedy matches Reoptimized plug-in and Oracle static, and its worst-target RMSE is 11%11\% to 18%18\% lower than those of Estimated static, Equal expenditure, and Cheapest only. At the smallest budget, B=500B=500, it has the smallest reported worst-target RMSE among the procedures, including Oracle static, although the Monte Carlo uncertainty is substantial at this budget. Figure 4 shows the purchased allocation approaching the optimal design, with the mass on Loggers 2 and 5 shrinking toward zero. Note that simple cost-based rules are far from optimal here. The criterion ratio 𝒢⁡(zθ)/𝒢⋆\mathcal{G}(z_{\theta})/\mathcal{G}^{\star}, where zθ=θ/c⊤​θz_{\theta}=\theta/c^{\top}\theta is the design with sample fractions θ\theta, is 2.502.50 for equal sample counts, 1.401.40 for Equal expenditure, and 1.211.21 for purchasing only from the cheapest logger.

6 Discussion

In this paper, we studied budgeted data acquisition in off-policy evaluation, in which observations are purchased sequentially from a fixed set of loggers with heterogeneous costs. We derived the Adaptive Greedy rule from the pooled efficiency bound of Kallus et al. (2021), and showed that each purchase is an approximate Frank–Wolfe step (Frank and Wolfe, 1956) on the worst-target criterion. We also showed that the purchased design converges to the minimax design. The pooled estimator computed from the purchased sample remains asymptotically normal, with variance equal to the fixed-design bound at the selected composition. Numerical studies show that the procedure matches the accuracy of repeated reoptimization at a fraction of its computational cost.

Three extensions remain open. First, we assumed that the logging probabilities are known. When they must be estimated, the estimation error enters both the purchasing rule and the final estimator, although the efficiency bound itself is unchanged (Kallus et al., 2021, Theorem 5). Second, inference for the final estimator relies on Assumption 5, and establishing it for common regression methods under adaptive sampling, in the spirit of Hadad et al. (2021) and Bibaut et al. (2021), would be useful. Finally, we assumed fixed prices per observation. When prices depend on the counts already purchased (variable pricing), the feasible set and its vertices move with the design, and extending the Frank–Wolfe argument to this setting remains an open and interesting problem.

Appendix A1 Notation and Overview

The appendices are organized as follows. Appendix A2 contains the derivations used in Section 3, and Appendices A3 and A4 prove the results of Sections 4.1 and 4.2. Auxiliary results are stated where they are first needed; those with longer proofs are proved in Appendix A6, in the order of logical dependence. Appendix A5 treats the block-split estimator, and Appendix A7 gives the details of the numerical studies.

Appendix A2 Derivations for Section 3

Appendix A3 Proofs for Section 4.1

This appendix proves Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.1. We first establish parts (i) and (ii) of the theorem along the infinite-budget sequence of Section 4.1, in which every logger is always available, and then transfer them to the budgeted algorithm. Auxiliary results are stated where they are first needed, and those not proved here are proved in Appendix A6.

A3.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Our argument goes through the infinite-budget sequence (K¯t,N¯t,C¯t)t≥n0(\bar{K}_{t},\bar{N}_{t},\bar{C}_{t})_{t\geq n_{0}} of Section 4.1. It follows Algorithm 1, but keeps every logger available at every step. Write 𝒯\mathcal{T} for its set of forced steps (those steps tt at which κ⁡(θ¯t)<χt\kappa(\bar{\theta}_{t})<\chi_{t}), z¯t=zN¯t\bar{z}_{t}=z_{\bar{N}_{t}}, and θ¯t=N¯t/t\bar{\theta}_{t}=\bar{N}_{t}/t; by (4.1),

z¯t+1=(1−γt)​z¯t+γt​vt,vt=eK¯t+1cK¯t+1,γt=cK¯t+1C¯t+1.\bar{z}_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_{t})\bar{z}_{t}+\gamma_{t}v_{t},\qquad v_{t}=\frac{e_{\bar{K}_{t+1}}}{c_{\bar{K}_{t+1}}},\qquad\gamma_{t}=\frac{c_{\bar{K}_{t+1}}}{\bar{C}_{t+1}}.

Along this sequence, we call a purchase satisfying (4.5), with ztz_{t} replaced by z¯t\bar{z}_{t}, a δt\delta_{t}-approximate conditional-gradient step. The proof rests on two results. The first is an infinite-budget version of the theorem, proved in Appendix A3.2; the second couples the two sequences, and is proved in Appendix A6. Unlike Theorem 4.1, which concerns the actual budgeted algorithm stopped at TBT_{B}, the following proposition establishes convergence and rates for the infinite-budget sequence, in which every logger remains affordable.

Proposition A3.1.

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 4.1 hold.

  1. (i)

    Almost surely,

    z¯t→z⋆andθ¯t→θ⋆,\bar{z}_{t}\to z^{\star}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bar{\theta}_{t}\to\theta^{\star}, (A3.1)

    and only finitely many steps of the infinite-budget sequence are forced.

  2. (ii)

    Under the additional conditions of part (ii) of Theorem 4.1, there are, on an event of probability one, finite random constants U¯𝒢\bar{U}_{\mathcal{G}}, U¯z\bar{U}_{z}, and U¯θ\bar{U}_{\theta} such that, for all sufficiently large tt,

    0≤𝒢(z¯t)−𝒢(z⋆)≤U¯𝒢C¯t−β,∥z¯t−z⋆∥2≤U¯zC¯t−β/2,∥θ¯t−θ⋆∥2≤U¯θC¯t−β/2.0\leq\mathcal{G}(\bar{z}_{t})-\mathcal{G}(z^{\star})\leq\bar{U}_{\mathcal{G}}\bar{C}_{t}^{-\beta},\qquad\|\bar{z}_{t}-z^{\star}\|_{2}\leq\bar{U}_{z}\bar{C}_{t}^{-\beta/2},\qquad\|\bar{\theta}_{t}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\leq\bar{U}_{\theta}\bar{C}_{t}^{-\beta/2}. (A3.2)

A3.2 Proof of Proposition A3.1

We first collect the results that the proof relies on: strong convexity of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, five properties of the smoothed criterion, control of the pooled coverage under forced sampling, and an elementary fact about recursions. Their proofs are given in Appendix A6. The proof also uses Lemma A3.10 of Appendix A3.3, by which unforced purchases are approximate conditional-gradient steps.

Recall that 𝒢=maxj⁡𝒢j\mathcal{G}=\max_{j}\mathcal{G}_{j}, where

𝒢j​(v)=Vj𝟏⊤​v+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)𝝁​(X,a)⊤​v,𝝁⁡(x,a)=(μ1​(a∣x),…,μK​(a∣x))⊤,v∈𝒞.\mathcal{G}_{j}(v)=\frac{V_{j}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}v}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{W_{j}(X,a)}{\bm{\mu}(X,a)^{\top}v},\qquad\bm{\mu}(x,a)=(\mu_{1}(a\mid x),\ldots,\mu_{K}(a\mid x))^{\top},\qquad v\in\mathcal{C}.

To bound the denominators, we restrict vv to designs with positive coverage on 𝒮\mathcal{S},

𝒞+={v∈𝒞:ess​inf(x,a)∈𝒮⁡𝝁​(x,a)⊤​v>0}=⋃e>0𝒞⁡(e),𝒞⁡(e)={v∈𝒞:ess​inf(x,a)∈𝒮⁡𝝁​(x,a)⊤​v≥e}.\mathcal{C}_{+}=\Big\{v\in\mathcal{C}:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}}\bm{\mu}(x,a)^{\top}v>0\Big\}=\bigcup_{e>0}\mathcal{C}(e),\qquad\mathcal{C}(e)=\Big\{v\in\mathcal{C}:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}}\bm{\mu}(x,a)^{\top}v\geq e\Big\}.

These sets are convex because 𝝁​(x,a)⊤​v\bm{\mu}(x,a)^{\top}v is linear in vv. Moreover, 𝝁​(x,a)⊤​v=(𝟏⊤​v)​mv/𝟏⊤​v​(a∣x)\bm{\mu}(x,a)^{\top}v=(\mathbf{1}^{\top}v)\,m_{v/\mathbf{1}^{\top}v}(a\mid x) and 𝟏⊤​v≥cmax−1\mathbf{1}^{\top}v\geq c_{\max}^{-1} on 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and so every v∈𝒞v\in\mathcal{C} with κ⁡(v/𝟏⊤​v)>0\kappa(v/\mathbf{1}^{\top}v)>0 lies in 𝒞⁡(e)\mathcal{C}(e) with e=κ⁡(v/𝟏⊤​v)/cmaxe=\kappa(v/\mathbf{1}^{\top}v)/c_{\max}.

Proposition A3.2.

Under Assumptions 1 and 3, for every v∈𝒞+v\in\mathcal{C}_{+} and every hh with c⊤​h=0c^{\top}h=0,

h⊤​∇2𝒢j​(v)​h≥2​cmin3​λj​‖h‖22.h^{\top}\nabla^{2}\mathcal{G}_{j}(v)h\geq 2c_{\min}^{3}\lambda_{j}\|h\|_{2}^{2}. (A3.3)

Consequently each 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}, and therefore 𝒢\mathcal{G}, is mm-strongly convex along every segment contained in 𝒞+\mathcal{C}_{+}, with m=2​cmin3​minj​λj>0m=2c_{\min}^{3}\min_{j}\lambda_{j}>0.

Strong convexity enters the argument only through the following quadratic growth around z⋆z^{\star}, which converts convergence of the criterion into convergence of the design.

Lemma A3.2.

Under Assumptions 1, 2, and 3, 𝒢⁡(v)−𝒢⁡(z⋆)≥m2​‖v−z⋆‖22\mathcal{G}(v)-\mathcal{G}(z^{\star})\geq\tfrac{m}{2}\|v-z^{\star}\|_{2}^{2} for every v∈𝒞v\in\mathcal{C}, so z⋆z^{\star} is the unique minimizer of 𝒢\mathcal{G} over 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

ωj​(v,ρ)=exp⁡{𝒢j​(v)/ρ}∑ℓexp⁡{𝒢ℓ​(v)/ρ}.\omega_{j}(v;\rho)=\frac{\exp\{\mathcal{G}_{j}(v)/\rho\}}{\sum_{\ell}\exp\{\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(v)/\rho\}}.

Under Assumption 1, parts (a), (b), (c), and (e) hold on 𝒞+\mathcal{C}_{+}, and part (d) holds on 𝒞⁡(e)\mathcal{C}(e) for every e∈(0,1]e\in(0,1].

Next, we control the coverage under forced sampling. The two lemmas below concern any sequence generated by Algorithm 1 during the steps at which every logger is affordable, in particular the infinite-budget sequence. Write θt=Nt/t\theta_{t}=N_{t}/t, call step tt forced if κ⁡(θt)<χt\kappa(\theta_{t})<\chi_{t}, and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of forced steps. For the analysis, let

so that the condition 0<χ0≤κ⁡(𝟏/K)/80<\chi_{0}\leq\kappa(\mathbf{1}/K)/8 of Section 3.3 reads 0<χ0≤κall/(8​K)0<\chi_{0}\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}/(8K). By definition of κall\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}, for every θ∈𝒮K\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{K} and every (x,a)∈𝒮(x,a)\in\mathcal{S},

mθ​(a∣x)≥(mink⁡θk)​∑k=1Kμk​(a∣x),κ⁡(θ)≥κall​mink​θk.m_{\theta}(a\mid x)\geq\left(\min_{k}\theta_{k}\right)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{k}(a\mid x),\qquad\kappa(\theta)\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}\min_{k}\theta_{k}. (A3.4)
Lemma A3.4.

Suppose 0<χ0≤κall/(8​K)0<\chi_{0}\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}/(8K), 0<υ<10<\upsilon<1, and the initialization purchases n0/K≥4n_{0}/K\geq 4 observations from each logger. Then, as long as every logger is affordable,

    κ⁡(θt)≥χt/2\kappa(\theta_{t})\geq\chi_{t}/2 for every t≥n0t\geq n_{0};

    each logger receives at most χt​t/κall+1\chi_{t}t/\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}+1 forced purchases at steps s≤ts\leq t, and ∑t∈𝒯γt<∞\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\gamma_{t}<\infty, where γt=cKt+1/Ct+1\gamma_{t}=c_{K_{t+1}}/C_{t+1}.

Summing part (b) over the KK loggers, the number of forced purchases up to time tt is at most K⁡(χt​t/κall+1)=O⁡(t1−υ)K(\chi_{t}t/\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}+1)=O(t^{1-\upsilon}), as stated in Section 3.3.

Lemma A3.5.

Under Assumption 2 and the conditions of Lemma A3.4, if θt→θ⋆\theta_{t}\to\theta^{\star} along a sequence in which every logger is always affordable, then only finitely many steps are forced, and κ⁡(θt)≥κ⋆/2\kappa(\theta_{t})\geq\kappa_{\star}/2 for all sufficiently large tt.

Computing pooled coverage.

When the context support is finite and known, κ⁡(θ)\kappa(\theta) can be computed by taking the minimum of mθ​(a∣x)m_{\theta}(a\mid x) over all target-relevant context-action pairs.

For general context spaces, forced sampling may instead use

κ~(θ)=ess​inf(x,a)∈𝒮∑k=1Kθkμ~k(a∣x),\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta)=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_{k}\widetilde{\mu}_{k}(a\mid x),

where the known functions μ~k\widetilde{\mu}_{k} satisfy 0≤μ~k≤μk0\leq\widetilde{\mu}_{k}\leq\mu_{k}. For example, we can partition 𝒮\mathcal{S} into finitely many disjoint measurable regions 𝒮1,…,𝒮R\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{R} of positive measure. For each logger kk and region rr, choose a known constant

0≤μ¯k,r≤ess​inf(x,a)∈𝒮r⁡μk​(a∣x),0\leq\underline{\mu}_{k,r}\leq\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}_{r}}\mu_{k}(a\mid x),

and set μ~k​(a∣x)=μ¯k,r\widetilde{\mu}_{k}(a\mid x)=\underline{\mu}_{k,r} for (x,a)∈𝒮r(x,a)\in\mathcal{S}_{r}. Then κ~​(θ)=min⁡∑k=1K1≤r≤R⁡θk​μ¯k,r≤κ⁡(θ).\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta)=\min_{1\leq r\leq R}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_{k}\underline{\mu}_{k,r}\leq\kappa(\theta). Thus, once the regional bounds are computed, evaluating κ~​(θ)\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta) requires only a finite minimum of weighted sums, with O⁡(K​R)O(KR) operations. For structured logging policies on bounded regions, such bounds can be obtained using interval methods (G.-Tóth et al., 2021). Individual regional bounds may be zero, so this construction does not require every logger to cover every target-relevant action.

This alternative requires κ~​(θ⋆)>0\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta^{\star})>0 and 0<χ0≤κ~​(𝟏/K)/80<\chi_{0}\leq\widetilde{\kappa}(\mathbf{1}/K)/8. Because κ~\widetilde{\kappa} is an infimum of the nonnegative linear functions θ↦∑kθk​μ~k​(a∣x)\theta\mapsto\sum_{k}\theta_{k}\widetilde{\mu}_{k}(a\mid x), it has the three properties of κ\kappa that the coverage proofs use:

κ~​(t​θ+ekt+1)≥tt+1​κ~​(θ),κ~​(θ)≥K​κ~​(𝟏/K)​mink​θk,|κ~​(θ)−κ~​(θ′)|≤‖θ−θ′‖1,\widetilde{\kappa}\Big(\frac{t\theta+e_{k}}{t+1}\Big)\geq\frac{t}{t+1}\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta),\qquad\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta)\geq K\widetilde{\kappa}(\mathbf{1}/K)\min_{k}\theta_{k},\qquad|\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta)-\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta^{\prime})|\leq\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{1},

the last because μ~k≤1\widetilde{\mu}_{k}\leq 1. The proofs of Lemmas A3.4 and A3.5 therefore go through with three substitutions. A step is forced if κ~​(θt)<χt\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta_{t})<\chi_{t}; K​κ~​(𝟏/K)K\widetilde{\kappa}(\mathbf{1}/K) replaces κall\kappa_{\mathrm{all}}, and (A3.4) holds with μ~k\widetilde{\mu}_{k} and κ~\widetilde{\kappa} in place of μk\mu_{k} and κ\kappa. Finally, κ~​(θ⋆)\widetilde{\kappa}(\theta^{\star}) replaces κ⋆\kappa_{\star} in the proof of Lemma A3.5. Since κ≥κ~\kappa\geq\widetilde{\kappa}, the remaining arguments are unchanged.

Appendix A4 Proofs for Section 4.2

This appendix proves Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.1. We compare J^B\widehat{J}_{B} with two averages that cannot be computed. Replacing q^B\widehat{q}_{B} by qq in (3.12) gives J~B=TB−1​∑i≤TBψi​(θ^B)\widetilde{J}_{B}=T_{B}^{-1}\sum_{i\leq T_{B}}\psi_{i}(\widehat{\theta}_{B}), and also replacing θ^B\widehat{\theta}_{B} by θ⋆\theta^{\star} gives J~B⋆=TB−1​∑i≤TBψi​(θ⋆)\widetilde{J}_{B}^{\star}=T_{B}^{-1}\sum_{i\leq T_{B}}\psi_{i}(\theta^{\star}). The error then splits as

J^B−J=(J^B−J~B)+(J~B−J~B⋆)+(J~B⋆−J).\widehat{J}_{B}-J=(\widehat{J}_{B}-\widetilde{J}_{B})+(\widetilde{J}_{B}-\widetilde{J}_{B}^{\star})+(\widetilde{J}_{B}^{\star}-J).

The last term is an average of martingale differences, and the middle term reflects the random denominator. Theorem A4.1 below shows that the former is asymptotically normal and the latter is op(TB−1/2)o_{p}(T_{B}^{-1/2}). The first term is the regression remainder ℛB​(θ^B)\mathcal{R}_{B}(\widehat{\theta}_{B}), which Assumption 5 controls. Beyond Assumptions 1 and 2, Theorem A4.1 uses only predictable logger selection and convergence of the final composition, so it also applies to other purchasing rules with these properties.

Throughout, for each budget BB, (ℱi)(\mathcal{F}_{i}) is the filtration of Section 2.1 for the sequence with that budget, extended by ℱi=ℱTB\mathcal{F}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{T_{B}} for i>TBi>T_{B}. Since each purchase costs at least cminc_{\min} and the total cost is at most BB, we have TB≤nBT_{B}\leq n_{B}, where nB=⌈B/cmin⌉n_{B}=\lceil B/c_{\min}\rceil. The event {i≤TB}\{i\leq T_{B}\} equals {B−Ci−1≥cmin}\{B-C_{i-1}\geq c_{\min}\}, so it is ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1}-measurable.

A4.1 Proof of Theorem 4.2

The key step is the following result, which we prove in Appendix A4.2.

Theorem A4.1.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, suppose θ^B→θ⋆\widehat{\theta}_{B}\to\theta^{\star} in probability. Then

  1. (i)

    TB​(J~B⋆−J)→N⁡{0,ΣA​(θ⋆)}\sqrt{T_{B}}(\widetilde{J}_{B}^{\star}-J)\to N\{0,\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star})\} in distribution;

  2. (ii)

    writing J~B=TB−1​∑i≤TBψi​(θ^B)\widetilde{J}_{B}=T_{B}^{-1}\sum_{i\leq T_{B}}\psi_{i}(\widehat{\theta}_{B}),

    in probability, and consequently TB​(J~B−J)→N⁡{0,ΣA​(θ⋆)}\sqrt{T_{B}}(\widetilde{J}_{B}-J)\to N\{0,\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star})\} in distribution.

Under the conditions of part (i) of Theorem 4.1, θ^B→θ⋆\widehat{\theta}_{B}\to\theta^{\star} almost surely. Theorem A4.1 therefore applies and gives TB​(J~B−J)→N⁡{0,ΣA​(θ⋆)}\sqrt{T_{B}}(\widetilde{J}_{B}-J)\to N\{0,\Sigma_{A}(\theta^{\star})\}, and it remains to show that the estimated regression does not change this limit. By definition, the jjth coordinate of J^B−J~B\widehat{J}_{B}-\widetilde{J}_{B} is ℛB,j​(θ^B)\mathcal{R}_{B,j}(\widehat{\theta}_{B}). On the event {∥θ^B−θ⋆∥2≤rB}\{\|\widehat{\theta}_{B}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\leq r_{B}\}, whose probability tends to one by Assumption 5,

maxj|ℛB,j(θ^B)|≤maxjsup‖θ−θ⋆‖2≤rB|ℛB,j(θ)|=op(TB−1/2).\max_{j}|\mathcal{R}_{B,j}(\widehat{\theta}_{B})|\leq\max_{j}\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\leq r_{B}}|\mathcal{R}_{B,j}(\theta)|=o_{p}(T_{B}^{-1/2}).

Hence TB​(J^B−J~B)→0\sqrt{T_{B}}(\widehat{J}_{B}-\widetilde{J}_{B})\to 0 in probability, and Slutsky’s theorem gives (4.10).

A4.4 Pooled Efficiency

The logger-specific estimator divides each observation by the propensity of the logger that generated it. At a fixed logger composition θ\theta, its covariance is

ΣL​(θ)=Cov⁡{qΠ​(X)}+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜σ2​(X,a)​π​(a∣X)​π​(a∣X)⊤​∑k=1Kθkμk​(a∣X),\Sigma_{L}(\theta)=\mathrm{Cov}\{q_{\Pi}(X)\}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sigma^{2}(X,a)\pi(a\mid X)\pi(a\mid X)^{\top}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\theta_{k}}{\mu_{k}(a\mid X)}, (A4.9)

whose jjth diagonal entry is

Lj​(θ)=Vj+𝔼X​∑a∈𝒜Wj​(X,a)​∑k=1Kθkμk​(a∣X).L_{j}(\theta)=V_{j}+\mathbb{E}_{X}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}W_{j}(X,a)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\theta_{k}}{\mu_{k}(a\mid X)}. (A4.10)

To derive (4.13), fix u∈ℝMu\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. The context terms of ΣA​(θ)\Sigma_{A}(\theta) and ΣL​(θ)\Sigma_{L}(\theta) coincide, so it suffices to compare the residual terms. For each (x,a)(x,a), Jensen’s inequality for the convex function y↦1/yy\mapsto 1/y, with 1/0=∞1/0=\infty, gives

1mθ​(a∣x)=1∑kθk​μk​(a∣x)≤∑k=1Kθkμk​(a∣x).\frac{1}{m_{\theta}(a\mid x)}=\frac{1}{\sum_{k}\theta_{k}\mu_{k}(a\mid x)}\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\theta_{k}}{\mu_{k}(a\mid x)}.

Taking u=eju=e_{j} gives Aj​(θ)≤Lj​(θ)A_{j}(\theta)\leq L_{j}(\theta). Appendix A5 A Block-Split Estimator

In the final estimator (3.12), q^B\widehat{q}_{B} is fitted on the same observations over which it is averaged, and the denominator mθ^Bm_{\widehat{\theta}_{B}} is random. The block-split estimator divides the sample into blocks of geometrically growing size, and evaluates each block with a regression fitted on earlier blocks and with its own realized logger frequencies in the denominator.

Fix n¯≥1\bar{n}\geq 1 and ϰ>1\varkappa>1 with (ϰ−1)​n¯≥1(\varkappa-1)\bar{n}\geq 1, let τ¯0=0\bar{\tau}_{0}=0 and τ¯ℓ=⌈ϰℓ−1​n¯⌉\bar{\tau}_{\ell}=\lceil\varkappa^{\ell-1}\bar{n}\rceil for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, and let

LB=max⁡{ℓ≥1:τ¯ℓ≤TB},τ0=0,τℓ=τ¯ℓ​(1≤ℓ<LB),τLB=TB.L_{B}=\max\{\ell\geq 1:\bar{\tau}_{\ell}\leq T_{B}\},\qquad\tau_{0}=0,\qquad\tau_{\ell}=\bar{\tau}_{\ell}\ (1\leq\ell<L_{B}),\qquad\tau_{L_{B}}=T_{B}. (A5.1)

The condition (ϰ−1)​n¯≥1(\varkappa-1)\bar{n}\geq 1 gives ϰℓ​n¯−ϰℓ−1​n¯≥1\varkappa^{\ell}\bar{n}-\varkappa^{\ell-1}\bar{n}\geq 1, so the τ¯ℓ\bar{\tau}_{\ell} strictly increase and every block is nonempty. Set ℬℓ={i:τℓ−1<i≤τℓ}\mathcal{B}_{\ell}=\{i:\tau_{\ell-1}<i\leq\tau_{\ell}\} and nℓ=|ℬℓ|n_{\ell}=|\mathcal{B}_{\ell}|. For ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, let q^(ℓ)\widehat{q}^{(\ell)} be fitted using only observations before block ℓ\ell, and let θ^k(ℓ)=nℓ−1∑i∈ℬℓ𝟏{Ki=k}\widehat{\theta}^{(\ell)}_{k}=n_{\ell}^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{\ell}}\mathbf{1}\{K_{i}=k\} be the logger proportions within block ℓ\ell. The block-split estimator is

J^B,jBS=1TB−τ1​∑ℓ=2LB∑i∈ℬℓ[q^j(ℓ)​(Xi)+πj​(Ai∣Xi)mθ^(ℓ)​(Ai∣Xi)​{Ri−q^(ℓ)​(Xi,Ai)}].\widehat{J}^{\mathrm{BS}}_{B,j}=\frac{1}{T_{B}-\tau_{1}}\sum_{\ell=2}^{L_{B}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{\ell}}\left[\widehat{q}^{(\ell)}_{j}(X_{i})+\frac{\pi_{j}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{m_{\widehat{\theta}^{(\ell)}}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}\{R_{i}-\widehat{q}^{(\ell)}(X_{i},A_{i})\}\right]. (A5.2)

The regression for block ℓ\ell is fixed before the block begins, and the denominator uses the block’s own logger frequencies. The construction is designed so that the regression error enters only through a martingale term.
